l_leucine.applicability_decision: Conflicting human evidence with no clear benefit, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. A meta-analysis of 17 RCTs found leucine alone had no effect on lean mass, handgrip or leg press in older adults (PMID 35845777). Free leucine added nothing to resistance training in young men (PMID 32079916), frail older women (PMID 40926079) or midlife women (PMID 31577520). Two small trials are positive: walking time in institutionalized older adults on 6 g/day (PMID 32230954) and fat-free mass during energy restriction on 3 g/day (PMID 37923932). An umbrella review favors leucine for muscle mass in sarcopenia without saying in its abstract whether that is free leucine (PMID 32483625), and a 2025 meta-analysis calls its evidence low quality and limited when leucine is used alone (PMID 40805998). The stored trials tested an amino acid mixture (PMID 16507602) and a whey drink (PMID 24284442), measuring protein synthesis over hours. The evidence conflicts with no clear benefit for the free leucine on these labels. PMID 35845777 states: 'Leucine-isolated supplementation did not improve muscle mass and strength in elderly.' These sources do not establish a universal standalone 2-3 g clinical threshold or general-population efficacy without the studied preparation and population context. All four labels print Omega-6 Fatty Acids as a summary row of an oil, not as an added active: EfaGold hemp oil 8.5 g, and MEGA 3/6/9 oil blend 705 mg on three labels, each with linoleic acid and gamma-linolenic acid rows beside it. The Cochrane review (30488422, 19 RCTs, 6461 participants, 12 of linoleic acid and 7 of supplemental gamma-linolenic acid) found increased omega-6 fats may make little or no difference to all-cause mortality or cardiovascular events. It also reports conflicting signals: a possible reduction in myocardial infarction (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.02, low quality) and lower total cholesterol. A later meta-analysis in atherosclerotic disease (38224465) found omega-6 had no significant effect on mortality or cardiovascular events, with low-quality evidence. A meta-analysis of linoleic acid trials (23386268) showed no cardiovascular benefit. So the evidence conflicts on surrogates with no clear clinical benefit. Most of these trials had omega-6 fats displacing saturated or monounsaturated fats at dietary amounts, so this is the best available evidence rather than a test of these exact products. This covers cardiovascular outcomes only; no on-target oral trial for the joint or skin purposes on some of these labels was found in what was read. Abstracts only. PMID 30488422 states: 'We found no evidence that increasing omega-6 fats reduces cardiovascular outcomes other than MI, where 53 people may need to increase omega-6 fat intake to prevent 1 person from experiencing MI.' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

coffeeberry.applicability_decision: Conflicting human evidence with no clear benefit, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. The one label, Neuro Shred, prints NeuroFactor 100 mg, dried whole coffee fruit concentrate, in a formula with three caffeine rows, Morosil, Capsimax and other actives. The on-target trial 37299382 gave 100 mg or 300 mg coffeeberry extract alone to 72 healthy adults in a double-blind crossover; 300 mg had no effect, and 100 mg increased mental fatigue and decreased accuracy on a sustained attention task, which the authors say to read with caution. It is acute and its abstract names no primary outcome. Other trials conflict. 33498314, a pilot crossover at 100 mg in older adults, reported decreased reaction time and increased BDNF. 39064791 at 200 mg reported better working memory accuracy against placebo. 31829793 reported shorter reaction time in 71 adults with mild cognitive decline with no main effect on accuracy and no amount in the abstract. 40993029 at 300 mg improved short passing only, and 34380382 at 1100 mg reported alerting effects with limited cognitive effects. The stored 23312069 is a single dose raising plasma BDNF 143% from baseline in 10 people, with no cognitive outcome. This is conflicting evidence with no clear benefit, and the labelled formula's caffeine rows can't be separated from the concentrate. Abstracts only. PMID 37299382 states: 'Overall, the findings of the current study suggest that coffeeberry extract at a low or moderate dose does not have a beneficial effect on mood, mental and physical energy levels, or cognition; higher doses, as have been administered previously, may be more effective.' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

studies.quote: Analysis revealed no effect of 300 mg coffeeberry extract, while 100 mg resulted in increased mental fatigue during the performance of cognitively demanding tasks (p = 0.025) and decreased accuracy on a task of sustained attention (p = 0.003), compared to placebo, at 60 min post dose.

d_beta_hydroxybutyrate_bhb.applicability_decision: Conflicting human evidence with no clear benefit, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. These 19 labels print beta-hydroxybutyrate mineral salts with no isomer stated: goBHB 4-in-1 ketone salt blends at 13,908 mg (266599, and 269325 and 306186 titled 11.7 g BHB) or unquantified in a matrix (268231, 326259), a 10 g three-mineral blend (219652), potassium and sodium salts at 12,973 mg BHB (77152), calcium salts at 6,541 mg (77111) or 1,238 mg (311247 to 311250), potassium at 9 g (266471, 270720), and magnesium at 7 g (269726) or 1,350 mg (329630, 329631, 329633, 329634). In healthy men, 11.38 g of BHB before exercise did not improve cycling or cognitive measures (29451991). In healthy men, 0.3 g/kg of ketone salts lowered time-trial power by about 7% (28750585). In 19 trained cyclists, two 0.38 g/kg doses did not change lactate, perceived exertion or efficiency, and 13 reported gastrointestinal symptoms (29338584). In 51 overweight or obese adults on a low-calorie diet, racemic BHB mineral salts twice daily for 8 weeks produced within-group fat loss, but group by time interactions for body composition were not significant (41305632). In a 24-hour crossover of 8 healthy adults, 38.7 g/day of ketone salts did not improve regulation of energy balance (37202059). A systematic review of 10 trials found that heterogeneity makes it difficult to conclude any benefit or detriment on physical performance (31586177). The evidence conflicts in two places: a 15-day placebo-controlled study of 86 patients with asthenia reported better cognition on BHB salts, with no primary outcome or dose in the abstract (39575959), and a 2026 meta-analysis found a modest cognitive improvement across exogenous ketones of all types, including esters, with no salt-specific estimate in the abstract (42063954). Abstracts only. PMID 29451991 states: 'In conclusion, βHB did not improve high-intensity cycling or cognitive performance measures; however, these findings might be partially explained by the absolute dosing protocol used for βHB in the present study as opposed to a relative (g/kg) dosing protocol used in previous research.' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

uva_ursi_leaf.applicability_decision: Conflicting human evidence with no clear benefit, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. These 11 labels print bearberry leaf extract at 750 mg with no ratio or standardization (311750, 311751, 311752, 311753, 252759, 254318, 254319, 254321), a 4:1 extract at 750 mg (331034), a 10:1 extract at 450 mg (306397), and uva ursi leaves at 1.11 g (304708). None prints an arbutin amount. In 382 women with acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection given a delayed antibiotic prescription, uva-ursi extract did not differ from placebo on frequency symptoms on days 2 to 4 (-0.06, 95% CI -0.33 to 0.21, p 0.661) and showed no evidence of reducing antibiotic use (30685500). In 398 women, uva ursi 105 mg, two tablets three times daily for 5 days, failed non-inferiority to fosfomycin on symptom burden (136.5%, margin 125%), with 8 versus 2 cases of pyelonephritis (p 0.067). The same trial did find 63.6% fewer antibiotic courses (34111592), the one positive result, which conflicts with 30685500 on antibiotic use. Abstracts only. PMID 30685500 states: 'We found no evidence of an effect of either intervention on the severity of frequency symptoms.' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

gamma_linolenic_acid.applicability_decision: Conflicting human evidence with no clear benefit, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. The 11 labels print GLA at 165 to 480 mg. Six name borage oil as the source (181851, 232718, 328569 as the row form; 223170, 218723, 77205 as a separate borage row), three carry it in a mixed omega blend that includes borage oil (304676, 327995, 332936), one prints safflower oil (65773) and one prints no source in an omega product (222789). For rheumatoid arthritis, Cochrane finds moderate evidence of some benefit from GLA oils (21328257), though the abstract states no doses. For eczema, oral borage and evening primrose oils lack effect (23633319). The one trial here with a named primary outcome and a label-range dose found 320 mg/day noninferior to alpha-lipoic acid on pain but not on total symptoms, with no placebo, in painful diabetic neuropathy (31701699), a purpose no label carries. Borage oil 1,000 mg lowered blood pressure against vitamin E (33534427). Borage oil at 880 mg GLA/day showed no effect on metabolic rate or BMI (34606560). A review of complementary medicines in rheumatoid arthritis found the available evidence does not support their current use (21652584), while Cochrane reports moderate evidence of some benefit from GLA oils (21328257), so the sources conflict. The one purpose with a positive pooled result rests on doses the abstract does not state. Abstracts only. PMID 23633319 states: 'Oral borage oil and evening primrose oil lack effect on eczema; improvement was similar to respective placebos used in trials.' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

lignans.applicability_decision: Finished review with no qualifying study for these labels, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. Six labels print Sesame Seed Lignan Extract at 10 to 20 mg, beside GLA, CLA blend or vitamin E rows, and three print HMRlignan Norway spruce lignan extract at 16.7 mg inside a chrysin, maca and nettle formula. No label prints flaxseed lignan or a sesamin amount. The stored trials tested flaxseed lignan, 360 mg/day in 17987126 with a modest HbA1c improvement and 50 mg/day SDG in 32575611 with no effect on bile acids, so they do not apply to these labels. For HMRlignan the one human study read, 24606716, is a single-blind dose comparison in 22 women at 36 and 72 mg/d with pharmacokinetic primary outcomes and no placebo; hot flashes fell within the high-dose group only. For sesame lignans, the trials read gave isolated sesamin at 60 mg/day (19352068, blood pressure fell, no primary outcome named) or 200 mg/day (31309643, inflammatory markers and tender joints improved in rheumatoid arthritis, no primary outcome named; 26151734, between-group differences in pressure and most lipids not significant). The meta-analysis 35311241 reports lower total cholesterol, LDL and systolic pressure across seven sesamin trials and 212 participants, but its abstract gives no dose and names no primary outcome. 26153159 tested sesame lignans at 10 mg combined with 55 mg alpha-tocopherol, near the sesame-plus-vitamin E labels, with no significant between-group difference in fatigue, sleep or appearance overall, a subgroup gain from age 40 and a rise in anti-oxidative capacity; a combination is not the ingredient alone. These reads are of abstracts only, and an abstract that names no primary outcome counts against qualifying for no credit. No study read meets the review's standard for what these labels print. This does not say the preparation was tested and failed. PMID 19352068 states: 'Twelve subjects were allocated to 4-wk intake of capsules with 60 mg sesamin per day and 13 subjects to 4-wk intake of a placebo (period 1).' Agent review (Claude), 2026-11-04; not clinician reviewed.

coffee_fruit.applicability_decision: Finished review with no qualifying study for these labels, so this review completes with no Evidence credit. The one label, CaffPhenol, prints CoffeeBerry Coffee, Coffea arabica whole fruit extract, at 143 mg, with Caffeine 100 mg under the words standardized to contain, and Suntheanine L-theanine 200 mg. It says the dose holds 100 mg of caffeine. The stored 23312069 gave a single 100 mg dose and reported plasma BDNF up 143% from baseline in 10 people, with no cognition or alertness measured and no primary outcome named. The closest caffeine-carrying trial, 42234539, gave a whole Coffea arabica cherry extract with 200 mg caffeine and 15 mg polyphenols to 12 cyclists and improved time trial work; it names no primary outcome, gives no extract mass, gives twice the caffeine, and tests exercise, a purpose this label does not carry. Trials of polyphenol-rich or decaffeinated extract fall short as a different preparation: 39064791 at 200 mg and 31829793 reported cognitive gains on selected measures and name no primary outcome. 37299382 gave coffeeberry extract standardized to 40% chlorogenic acid at 100 and 300 mg and its authors report no beneficial effect on mood, energy or cognition, but it is not plainly this caffeine-standardized extract, and it names no primary outcome. No trial read tests the extract with theanine. These reads are of abstracts only, and an abstract that names no primary outcome counts against qualifying for no credit. No study read meets the review's standard for what these labels print. This does not say the preparation was tested and failed.
